mainTopic: Freeing half a slave: רבה's limit on the מחלוקת, the two ברייתות about giving property to slaves, and the half-slave's daily status
overview: The amud opens by finishing an answer: a person can be half slave and half free when two partners own a slave and one of them frees his share, and everyone agrees about that case. רבה then says that רבי and רבנן argue about freeing half a slave only when the master keeps the other half. If the master sells or gives away the other half, everyone agrees the freeing works. אביי challenges this with two ברייתות about a master who gives his property to two slaves: one says they free each other, the other says they get nothing. The גמרא offers several ways to settle the clash: 'all of it' versus 'half and half', one document versus two, and giving at the same time versus one after the other. The timing answer is rejected. רב אשי suggests that calling them 'my slaves' shows the master did not mean to free them, but רפרם proves from a משנה that 'my slave' can just mean 'who was my slave'. The גמרא then turns to a half-slave gored by an ox: the payment follows whose day it was, but marriage prohibitions do not switch by the day. Finally, a ברייתא about an ox that killed a half-slave is brought to test the day-by-day rule, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The half-slave is one owned by two partners
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its answer. A half-slave, half-free person can exist when two partners own a slave and one of them frees his share. Everyone agrees about that case.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is a slave owned by two partners, and in that case everyone agrees.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer from the previous page. It explains how a חצי עבד חצי בן חורין can exist even according to רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to how רב יוסף reads רבנן, one master cannot free only half of his slave. So the גמרא needed a case where half-freedom still happens. When two partners own a slave and one frees his half, the freeing works according to everyone, because that partner owns only that half.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is half slave and half free

phrases.english: With a slave belonging to two partners,
phrases.notes: This finishes an answer from the previous page: the half-slave case is one where a single partner freed his own share.

phrases.english: and that is everyone's opinion.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעֶבֶד שֶׁל שְׁנֵי שׁוּתָּפִין, וְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the question-and-answer from the previous page about how half-freedom can exist according to רבנן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the case in a specific situation (a jointly owned slave)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: According to רבנן, there seemed to be no way for someone to end up half slave and half free.
steps.terutzMaskana: When one partner frees his share of a jointly owned slave, half-freedom exists according to everyone.

steps.title: רבה limits the dispute to a master who keeps the other half
steps.stepSummary: רבה says רבי and רבנן argue only when the master frees half and keeps the other half. If he sells or gives away the other half, the slave no longer belongs to him at all, and everyone agrees the half-freedom works.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: The dispute is when the master freed half the slave and kept the other half. But if he freed half and sold or gave away the other half, the whole slave has left his ownership, so everyone agrees the slave acquired his half-freedom.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה sets the borders of the מחלוקת between רבי and רבנן about freeing half a slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה separates two cases. In the first, the master still holds part of the slave, and that is where רבי and רבנן argue. In the second, the master gives up the slave completely, half to freedom and half to someone else, and רבה says the freeing works according to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: He left it as it was, and kept it
Since all of him leaves the master's ownership

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a new rule that could shrink the מחלוקת a lot. That is exactly what אביי will now test.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
The dispute is when he freed half of him
phrases.notes: The dispute meant here is the one between רבי and רבנן about whether a master can free half his slave.

phrases.english: and left the other half of him.
But if he freed half of him and sold half of him,
or gave half of him as a gift,
since he goes out from him entirely,
everyone agrees he acquired.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: מַחֲלוֹקֶת – בְּשֶׁשִּׁיחְרֵר חֶצְיוֹ וְהִנִּיחַ חֶצְיוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new discussion about how far the מחלוקת of רבי and רבנן reaches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי and רבנן argue only when the master keeps the other half. If the master gives up the whole slave, everyone agrees the half-freedom works.

steps.title: אביי brings two ברייתות that seem to contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks whether רבי and רבנן really don't argue when the whole slave leaves the master. He quotes two ברייתות about a master giving his property to two slaves. One says they acquire and free each other. The other says they acquire nothing, not even themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Do they really not argue when the whole slave is given away? But one ברייתא teaches: If someone writes his property to his two slaves, they acquire it and free each other. And another ברייתא teaches: If someone says, 'All my property is given to so-and-so and so-and-so, my slaves,' they do not acquire even themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's rule by quoting two ברייתות that disagree about a case where the master gives away the whole slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a master gives everything to two slaves, each slave gets half of himself and half of the other slave. So the master gives up each slave completely, which is exactly רבה's 'everyone agrees' case. Yet the two ברייתות give opposite rulings, which suggests there is a real disagreement even here.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is taught (introduces a source used as a challenge)
One who writes over his property in a document

steps.confusionAlert: Each slave receives half of himself and half of his fellow slave. That is why this counts as the master giving up the whole slave, even though no single person gets all of either slave.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
And regarding all of him, they don't disagree?!
phrases.notes: He means the case where the master gives away the whole slave, half to freedom and half to someone else.

phrases.english: But one ברייתא teaches:
One who writes his property to his two slaves:
they acquired it, and they free each other.
phrases.notes: Each slave now owns half of the other slave, so each one can finish freeing the other.

phrases.english: And another ברייתא teaches: One who says,
"All my property is given to so-and-so
and so-and-so, my slaves":
they did not acquire even themselves.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: וּבְכוּלּוֹ – לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly challenges רבה's statement in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that everyone agrees when the master gives up the whole slave
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two ברייתות rule in opposite ways about a case where the whole slave leaves the master. That points to a real מחלוקת in exactly the case רבה said everyone agrees on.

steps.title: אביי explains the ברייתות as following רבי and רבנן
steps.stepSummary: אביי completes his challenge. The natural way to settle the two ברייתות is that the first follows רבי and the second follows רבנן. So רבי and רבנן do argue even when the whole slave leaves the master.
steps.simpleTranslation: What, is it not that this ברייתא follows רבי, and that ברייתא follows רבנן?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי finishes his attack by suggesting how to explain the two ברייתות, and that explanation goes against רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא, where the slaves go free, fits רבי, who holds that freeing half a slave works. The second ברייתא, where nothing works, fits רבנן, who hold that it does not. If that is right, רבי and רבנן argue even when the master keeps nothing, and רבה's rule falls.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not...? (introduces a suggested reading)

steps.whatToRemember: רבה says רבי and רבנן argue only when the master keeps half of the slave. אביי challenges this with two clashing ברייתות about giving property to two slaves. He reads them as רבי against רבנן, which would mean they argue even when the master gives up the whole slave.

phrases.english: What, is it not
that this one is רבי, and that one is the Rabbis?!
phrases.notes: "This one" is the first ברייתא, where the slaves free each other. "That one" is the second, where they get nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי, לָאו הָא רַבִּי, וְהָא רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion of אביי's challenge from the two ברייתות quoted in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that everyone agrees when the master gives up the whole slave
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the clashing ברייתות are explained as רבי against רבנן, then the two do argue in a case where the master keeps nothing, which contradicts רבה.

steps.title: Both ברייתות follow רבנן: 'all of it' versus 'half and half'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers אביי. Both ברייתות follow רבנן. The first is where the master gave all his property to each slave. The second is where he gave half to one and half to the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Both ברייתות follow רבנן. The first one is where the master said 'all of it' to each slave. The second one is where he said 'half to this one, half to that one.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects אביי's claim that the two ברייתות must be split between רבי and רבנן. It explains them as two different cases, and both cases follow רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both ברייתות are רבנן, there is no proof that רבי and רבנן argue when the whole slave leaves the master, so רבה's statement survives. When each slave gets 'all of it,' each one acquires and goes free. When each gets only 'half,' each slave ends up with only half of himself, and they do not acquire.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this one and that one
All of it: the master gave all his property to each slave
Half and half: the master gave half to one slave and half to the other

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. 'כולו' means each slave was given everything. 'חצי חצי' means the property was split between them. The whole answer depends on this difference.

phrases.english: No, both this and that follow the Rabbis;
this one is where he said "all of it,"
phrases.notes: He means the master gave all his property to each slave, and that property includes the other slave.

phrases.english: that one is where he said "half, half."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge from Step 4 by changing which cases the ברייתות are talking about.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the two ברייתות describe different situations rather than different opinions.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות contradict each other, so one must be רבי and one must be רבנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both ברייתות follow רבנן. They describe different cases: 'all of it' versus 'half and half.'

steps.title: The end of the second ברייתא suggests its beginning is the 'all of it' case
steps.stepSummary: The end of the second ברייתא says that 'half and half' does not work. That implies the beginning of that same ברייתא is about 'all of it,' and it also says they do not acquire.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the end of the second ברייתא says: 'If he said half and half, they did not acquire.' So the beginning must be about where he said 'all of it.' That means even 'all of it' does not work there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 5 using the wording of the second ברייתא itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The end of the second ברייתא mentions 'half and half' as a separate case. That suggests the beginning is a different case, namely 'all of it.' If so, the second ברייתא rules that even 'all of it' does not work, and the first ברייתא says it does work. The two ברייתות contradict each other again.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a source
The first part of a source
By implication, it can be inferred

phrases.english: But from the fact that the last clause teaches:

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אָמַר חֲצִי חֲצִי – לֹא קָנוּ,
phrases.english: "And if he said half, half, they did not acquire,"
it follows that the first clause is where he said "all of it"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case split from Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 5 that the second ברייתא is only about 'half and half.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second ברייתא's end clause names 'half and half' as a new case. That implies its beginning is the 'all of it' case, which brings back the contradiction with the first ברייתא.

steps.title: The end clause is only explaining the beginning
steps.stepSummary: The end of the second ברייתא is not a new case. It explains the beginning: 'they did not acquire even themselves' refers to the 'half and half' case.
steps.simpleTranslation: The end clause is explaining the beginning: 'They did not acquire even themselves.' How so? For example, where he said 'half and half.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It reads the second ברייתא as one case, with the end clause explaining the beginning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The end clause does not add a second case, so nothing implies the beginning is about 'all of it.' The whole second ברייתא is about 'half and half.' The split from Step 5 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is explaining, not adding a new case

phrases.english: It is explaining:
"They did not acquire even themselves." How so?
For example, where he said half, half.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from Step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the text: the end clause explains the beginning instead of adding a new case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The end clause is a separate case, so the beginning must be 'all of it.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The end clause defines the beginning. The whole second ברייתא is about 'half and half.'

steps.title: Logic supports reading the second ברייתא as one case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a logical support. If the beginning were 'all of it' and even that does not work, there would be no need to say that 'half and half' does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense. If you thought the beginning was about 'all of it,' then once it said that even 'all of it' does not work, why would it need to say that 'half and half' does not work?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings logic to support the answer in Step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Half and half' is the weaker case. If even 'all of it' fails, the weaker case obviously fails too, so stating it would add nothing. That suggests the end clause is not a separate case. It must be explaining the beginning.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it makes sense: a phrase that brings logical support
It enters your mind, if you would think

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable,
for if it enters your mind
that the first clause is where he said "all of it,"
now if when he said "all of it" they did not acquire,
is it necessary to say so when he said half, half?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the reading from Step 7.
steps.raayaObject: The reading that the second ברייתא's end clause explains its beginning, so the whole ברייתא is about 'half and half.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: Logic: a ברייתא would not state an obvious weaker case right after a stronger one.

steps.title: The logical support is pushed away: the end clause could reveal the beginning
steps.stepSummary: The support from Step 8 is not convincing. The ברייתא could state 'half and half' at the end to show that the beginning was about 'all of it,' and that even then they do not acquire.
steps.simpleTranslation: That reason proves nothing. The end clause may be there to show what the beginning means. Otherwise you might think the beginning is about 'half and half,' and that with 'all of it' they would acquire. So the end clause states 'half and half,' which shows the beginning is about 'all of it.' And even so, they do not acquire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the logical support from Step 8 by giving another reason the end clause might be needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A clause that seems unnecessary can still serve a purpose: it can show what the earlier clause is talking about. Read this way, the end clause shows that the beginning is the 'all of it' case. That reopens the possibility that the second ברייתא rules even 'all of it' fails. Only the support is knocked out, not the answer from Step 7 itself.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not a proof, that reason does not decide it
So that you should not say

steps.confusionAlert: This rejection only knocks out the logical support from Step 8. It does not prove the answer in Step 7 wrong. It only shows that Step 8's logic does not force that reading.

phrases.english: If it is because of this, it is no proof:
he taught the last clause to reveal the first clause,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא תֹּאמַר: רֵישָׁא דְּאָמַר חֲצִי חֲצִי,
phrases.english: so that you should not say: the first clause is where he said half, half,
but if he said "all of it" they acquire;
so he taught a last clause where he said half, half,
which implies that the first clause is where he said "all of it,"
and even so they did not acquire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the logical support brought in Step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the logical support from Step 8. The answer in Step 7 is left standing but without that support.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Step 8 assumed an obvious weaker case would never be stated. In fact it can be stated to show what the earlier clause is talking about.
steps.whatToRemember: The second ברייתא can be read two ways. Either the whole ברייתא is about 'half and half' (Step 7), or its beginning is about 'all of it' and the end clause is there to show that (Step 9). The logical support for the first reading has been pushed away.

steps.title: Another answer: one document versus two documents
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a different answer. The ברייתא that says the slaves did not acquire is about one document. The ברייתא that says they did acquire is about two documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it is not difficult: here it is one document, there it is two documents.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a brand-new way to settle the contradiction between the two ברייתות. The difference is how many documents the master wrote.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answer split the cases by 'all' versus 'half and half.' This answer splits them by the number of שטרות instead. If everything is in one שטר, the slaves do not acquire. If there is a separate שטר for each slave, they do acquire.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces another possible answer

phrases.english: And if you want, say: it is not difficult:
Here, it is in one document,
phrases.notes: This 'here' is the ברייתא that says they did not acquire.

phrases.english: there, it is in two documents.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second way, instead of Steps 5-9, to resolve the contradiction between the ברייתות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different case setup (one document versus two documents)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seem to argue about the same case.
steps.terutzMaskana: One ברייתא is about one שטר and does not work. The other is about two שטרות and does work.

steps.title: Why mention half and half if one document never works?
steps.stepSummary: If the second ברייתא is about one document, even giving 'all' does not work. So why does it bother to say 'half and half' does not work?
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is one document, why mention specifically half and half? Even if he said all of it, they also do not acquire!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new answer. It points out that the second ברייתא's mention of 'half and half' seems pointless under this answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the new answer, one שטר fails no matter what. So 'all of it' fails, and 'half and half' surely fails too. Spelling out 'half and half' adds nothing, so the answer seems not to fit the wording of the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Half and half: half to each slave

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁטָר אֶחָד, מַאי אִירְיָא חֲצִי חֲצִי?
phrases.english: If it is in one document, why specifically half and half?
Even if he said all of it
they also do not acquire!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁטָר אֶחָד, מַאי אִירְיָא חֲצִי חֲצִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of Step 10 from the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The one-document versus two-documents answer of Step 10
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If one שטר always fails, the ברייתא's specific mention of 'half and half' has no purpose.

steps.title: The ברייתא teaches two separate rules
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא means: with one document they never acquire. With two documents they do acquire. But if he said 'half and half,' then even two documents do not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is also what it is saying: they did not acquire even themselves. When is this said? With one document. But with two documents they acquired. And if he said half and half, even with two documents they also did not acquire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by reading the ברייתא as teaching two different rules. 'Half and half' is the case where even two documents fail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening line of the ברייתא is about one שטר, where nothing works. The ending about 'half and half' is a new rule. It teaches that even with two שטרות, giving each slave only half does not work. So 'half and half' is not pointless after all.

keyTerms.meaning: That is also what it is saying: introduces a reading of the source
In what case is this said?

phrases.english: That is also what it is saying:
They did not acquire even themselves,
In what case is this said? With one document,
but with two documents, they acquired;
and if he said half and half,

phrases.aramaic: אַף בִּשְׁנֵי שְׁטָרוֹת נָמֵי לָא קָנוּ.
phrases.english: even with two documents they also did not acquire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 11 and saves the answer of Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the ברייתא as two separate rules
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Half and half' seemed to repeat what one שטר already teaches.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Half and half' teaches that even two שטרות fail when each slave gets only half.

steps.title: Another answer: at the same time versus one after the other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a third answer. The ברייתא that says they acquired is when the documents were given at the same time. The one that says they did not acquire is when they were given one after the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it is not difficult: here it is at the same time, there it is one after the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives yet another way to settle the contradiction, this time based on timing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer says the key difference is when the master handed over the שטרות. Given together, they work. Given one after the other, they do not.

phrases.english: And if you want, say: it is not difficult:
here, it is at the same time,
phrases.notes: This 'here' is the ברייתא that says they did acquire.

phrases.english: there, it is one after the other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a third alternative resolution of the contradiction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different case setup (timing of giving the documents)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתות seem to argue about the same case.
steps.terutzMaskana: Giving at the same time works. Giving one after the other does not.

steps.title: The first slave should still acquire
steps.stepSummary: If the documents were given one after the other, the second slave fails because the first already owns him. But the first slave should acquire himself and his friend!
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, the last one does not acquire, because the first already acquired him. But the first should acquire himself and acquire his friend!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the timing answer. It shows that giving one after the other still works for the first slave, so it cannot explain a ruling of 'they did not acquire.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first slave to get his שטר receives all the property, which includes himself and the other slave. So he should go free and own the other slave. Only the second slave loses out, but the ברייתא says neither acquires.

phrases.english: Granted, the last one does not acquire,
because the first one already acquired him;
phrases.notes: The second slave was part of 'all the property' the first slave already received.

phrases.english: but the first one should acquire himself
and acquire his friend!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the timing answer of Step 13.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Giving one after the other still lets the first slave acquire, so it cannot explain a ruling that neither slave acquires.

steps.title: Back to the earlier answer
steps.stepSummary: Since the timing answer fails, the גמרא concludes that the correct answer is the one given earlier.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is clear as we answered at first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the timing answer and returns to its earlier explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question in Step 14 has no answer, so the timing explanation is rejected. The earlier way of settling the two ברייתות remains the accepted one.
steps.whatToRemember: The two ברייתות do not truly argue; each describes a different case. The timing answer was rejected, so the גמרא keeps the earlier explanation.

phrases.english: Rather, it is clear as we answered at first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of Step 14 and abandons the answer of Step 13.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The timing answer is rejected; the earlier resolution of the two ברייתות stands.

steps.title: רב אשי: The Master Called Them 'My Slaves'
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי settles the contradiction between the ברייתות. In the second ברייתא the master called them 'my slaves,' which shows he did not mean to free them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: It is different there, because the master calls them 'my slaves.'
steps.whatsHappening: After the timing answer failed, רב אשי offers a new way to settle the two clashing ברייתות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא where the slaves do not acquire, the master wrote 'my slaves.' Using that word shows he still sees them as his slaves, so he never meant to free them. In the other ברייתא he did not use that word, so they do acquire.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It is different there,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the second ברייתא, where the slaves did not acquire.

phrases.english: because he calls them 'my slaves.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers another way to resolve אביי's contradiction between the two ברייתות (steps 3-4), based on the master's wording 'my slaves'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות truly contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wording 'my slaves' shows the master meant to keep them as slaves, so in that case they do not go free.

steps.title: רפרם: 'My Slaves' May Mean Former Slaves
steps.stepSummary: רפרם challenges רב אשי. 'My slaves' could simply mean 'the ones who were my slaves until now.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רפרם said to רב אשי: But maybe 'my slaves' means those who already were his slaves before.
steps.whatsHappening: רפרם pushes back on רב אשי's answer. He says the word 'my slaves' does not prove anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי read 'my slaves' as 'they stay my slaves.' רפרם says it could just describe who they were up to now, like a label. If so, the word does not show the master wanted to keep them as slaves.

phrases.english: Rafram said to Rav Ashi:
But maybe 'my slaves' means those who already were!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַפְרָם לְרַב אָשֵׁי: וְדִלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב אשי's reading of the word 'my slaves.'
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that 'my slaves' shows the master meant to keep them enslaved
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word can just describe their past status, so it proves nothing about what the master intends now.

steps.title: רפרם Brings a משנה About Writing All Property to a Slave
steps.stepSummary: רפרם quotes a משנה. A master who writes all his property to his slave frees him, unless he holds back some land. רבי שמעון says the slave is free unless the master says 'except one ten-thousandth.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't we learn in a משנה: One who writes all his property to his slave, the slave goes free. If he held back any amount of land, the slave does not go free. רבי שמעון says: He is always free, unless the master says, 'All my property is given to so-and-so my slave, except for one part in ten thousand of it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רפרם is setting up a proof for his challenge. He quotes a משנה whose wording he will analyze in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the master gives everything, the slave is included in 'everything,' so he gets himself and goes free. If the master keeps back even a little, maybe the slave is part of what he kept. רבי שמעון says only the specific phrase 'except one ten-thousandth' keeps the slave from going free.

keyTerms.meaning: He has gone out to freedom
He held back / kept some for himself

phrases.english: Didn't we learn:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in פאה (3:8).

phrases.english: One who writes all his property to his slave –
he goes out to freedom;
if he held back any amount of land –
he does not go out to freedom.
Rabbi Shimon says:
He is always a free man,
until he says:
'All my property is given to so-and-so my slave,
except for one ten-thousandth of it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי לָא תְּנַן: הַכּוֹתֵב כׇּל נְכָסָיו לְעַבְדּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source that will back up רפרם's challenge.
steps.raayaObject: That 'my slave' can mean 'the one who was my slave'
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in פאה, the opinion of רבי שמעון

steps.title: Proof: 'My Slave' Means 'Who Was My Slave'
steps.stepSummary: From רבי שמעון we learn that without 'except one ten-thousandth,' the slave acquires even though the master called him 'my slave.' So 'my slave' must mean 'who was my slave,' and the same is true of 'my slaves.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason he does not go free is that the master said 'except one ten-thousandth of it.' So if he did not say that, the slave acquires. But why? The master called him 'slave'! It must be that 'my slave' means the one who was already my slave. Here too, 'my slaves' means those who were already my slaves.
steps.whatsHappening: רפרם finishes his proof from the משנה and uses it to knock down רב אשי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבי שמעון's case the master wrote 'so-and-so my slave,' and the slave still goes free as long as nothing was held back. So the word 'my slave' did not stop him from going free; it only described his past status. The same must be true for 'my slaves' in the ברייתא, so רב אשי's answer fails.

keyTerms.meaning: But if he did not say this

steps.confusionAlert: רפרם is not arguing with רבי שמעון. He is using רבי שמעון's own case to show that the word 'my slave' does not keep someone a slave.
steps.whatToRemember: Calling someone 'my slave' in a gift document does not by itself mean he stays a slave. It can simply mean 'the one who was my slave.' So רב אשי's answer does not stand.

phrases.english: The reason is because he said
['except for one ten-thousandth of it'],
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are part of the corrected wording.

phrases.english: but if he did not say this – he acquires;
why? He calls him 'slave'!
Rather, 'my slave' means who already was,
here too, 'my slaves' means who already were.

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּאָמַר חוּץ מֵאֶחָד מֵרִבּוֹא שֶׁבָּהֶן, הָא לָא אָמַר הָכִי קָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the inference from the משנה just quoted and applies it against רב אשי.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב אשי's answer to the contradiction between the ברייתות
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word 'my slave' does not show the master meant to keep him a slave, as רבי שמעון's case proves.

steps.title: Half-Slave Gored by an Ox: Payment Follows the Day
steps.stepSummary: If an ox gores the half-slave half-free man on his master's day, the payment goes to the master. On his own day, it goes to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If an ox gored him: on his master's day, the payment goes to his master; on his own day, it goes to himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic. It brings a teaching about a person who is half slave and half free and works for himself and his master on alternating days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This person's time is split: some days belong to his master and some to himself. The damage payment follows the owner of that day, so it is treated as if he is fully a slave on one day and fully free on the next.

phrases.english: If an ox gored him;
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the person who is half slave and half free, who splits his days between his master and himself.

phrases.english: on his master's day – it goes to his master,
on his own day – it goes to himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: נְגָחוֹ שׁוֹר; יוֹם שֶׁל רַבּוֹ לְרַבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about the half-slave half-free man.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Damages paid for injuring a half-slave go to whoever owns the day on which the injury happened.

steps.title: Then He Should Marry Differently Each Day
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule. If he is a slave on his master's days and free on his own days, he should be able to marry a שפחה on one day and a free woman on the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, on his master's day let him marry a maidservant, and on his own day let him marry a free woman!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the day-by-day idea to an extreme to test it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each day fully decides his status, marriage should follow the same pattern. That leads to a strange result, and it clashes with the משנה, which says he cannot marry anyone.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so / according to this logic

phrases.english: But if so –
on his master's day let him marry a maidservant,

phrases.aramaic: יוֹם שֶׁל עַצְמוֹ יִשָּׂא בַּת חוֹרִין!
phrases.english: on his own day let him marry a free woman!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה יוֹם שֶׁל רַבּוֹ יִשָּׂא שִׁפְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the day-by-day rule from the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that his status switches each day
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If his status switches daily, his marriage rules should switch too, which is absurd and goes against the משנה.

steps.title: The Daily Split Does Not Apply to Prohibitions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the day-by-day split covers money matters, not אסורים such as whom he may marry.
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not say this about prohibitions.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting the day-by-day rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Splitting by days works for money, like who gets the damage payment. For אסורים such as marriage, he stays half slave and half free all the time, so neither kind of marriage is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: A prohibition (as opposed to money matters)

steps.whatToRemember: For a half-slave, money follows the day; prohibitions do not. His marriage status stays mixed every day.

phrases.english: Regarding prohibitions we do not say this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the marriage challenge by limiting the scope of the rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule's scope (money vs. prohibitions)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: His status fully switches each day for everything.
steps.terutzMaskana: The daily split applies only to money matters, not to prohibitions like marriage.

steps.title: An ox that killed a half-slave half-free man pays half the fine to the master
steps.stepSummary: Using תא שמע, the גמרא quotes a ברייתא. When an ox kills a half-slave half-free man, the owner pays half the קנס to the master. This seems to challenge the day-by-day rule from Step 20.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if an ox killed a man who is half slave and half free, the ox's owner gives half of the fine to his master.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to test the rule from Step 20. That rule said the payment depends on whose day the goring happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 said that on the master's day everything goes to the master, and on the slave's own day everything goes to the slave. This ברייתא does not mention days at all. It splits the payment in half, giving the master half of the slave's fixed קנס, which seems to go against the day-by-day approach.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Come and hear', the גמרא is bringing a source to prove or challenge something
it killed (here, an ox killed a person)
a fixed fine set by the תורה, not based on actual value. For a slave killed by an ox it is thirty שקלים

steps.confusionAlert: 'Half a קנס' does not mean half the man's value. It means half of the fixed thirty-שקל slave fine, which comes to fifteen שקלים.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If [an ox] killed one who is half slave
phrases.notes: The ברייתא doesn't say 'ox', but it's talking about an ox that kills a person (שמות 21:28-32).

phrases.english: and half free man –
he gives half the fine to his master,
phrases.notes: The fine for a slave killed by an ox is thirty שקלים (שמות 21:32), so half is fifteen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the side discussion about marriage in Steps 21-22, the גמרא goes back to test the payment rule from Step 20 against a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule in Step 20 that an ox's payment goes fully to the master or fully to the slave, depending on whose day it was.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא splits the payment in half, giving half the קנס to the master, and does not make it depend on the day. This seems to contradict the day-based rule.
